title: Weight-Constrained Simple Path Enumeration in Weighted Graph

problem.claim: Given two query vertices and a weight threshold, identify all simple paths whose weight does not exceed the threshold.

gap.claim: Existing join-based path-enumeration solutions work only for unweighted graphs.

contributions.claim: A join-based framework for path enumeration in weighted graphs.
Novel data structures and operations based on the join-based framework, designed using characteristics of DFS.
A solution combining the advantages of join-based methods and DFS.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly state that this is the first join-based framework for weighted graphs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments were conducted on several real large graphs.
On weighted graphs, the method is reported to be much more efficient than existing algorithms.
On unweighted graphs, the method is reported to remain competitive with the state-of-the-art unweighted-graph solution.

narrative_sequence.summary: Path enumeration is presented as a fundamental, extensively studied problem.
The task is to enumerate all simple paths between two query vertices under a weight threshold.
Prior approaches include DFS-based and join-based solutions, but join-based solutions are limited to unweighted graphs.
The paper introduces a weighted-graph join framework, adds DFS-inspired data structures and operations, and combines join with DFS.
Experiments on real large graphs report improved efficiency for weighted graphs and competitiveness for unweighted graphs.

source_observation.claim: A join-based framework is extended from unweighted to weighted path enumeration and augmented with DFS-inspired operations.

interpretation.claim: Combining complementary algorithmic paradigms can address a limitation of an existing framework.

application.claim: When adapting an algorithm to a richer input setting, combine the scalable structure of an existing method with operations suited to the new constraints.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the combined design is preferable across all graph types or workloads.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the algorithmic complexity or detailed data-structure and operation designs.
The abstract does not identify the graph datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or experimental conditions.
